paragraphs: A community of the Ananites and the Karaites do affirm the probative force of ijmāʿ in several of the farāʾiḍ, and hold that ijmāʿ is one of the routes by which one comes to know the affirmative commandments. Their position is that the routes to knowledge of the affirmative commandments are three: the explicit text (al-naṣṣ), analogy (al-qiyās), and consensus (al-ijmāʿ). Some of them call this last route naql (transmission).[{2}] When they were pressed (by Rabbanite interlocutors) on the question: What is your definition of "sound" naql and ijmāʿ, given that you see the Rabbanites adducing ijmāʿ and naql for their positions, and yet you disagree with the Rabbanites on much, while still affirming the validity of the principle? — they answered: the sound ijmāʿ is what the Jewish denominations as a whole — Rabbanites, Ananites, Daudites, and the other sects — agree upon. They enumerate the sects one by one. They held that the sound ijmāʿ is precisely what all these factions together agree on; whatever is not held by all of them is not sound ijmāʿ.

The Rabbanite opponents replied to them: tell us — before the emergence of Anan, Benjamin, and the other sects you have just enumerated, was there a sound ijmāʿ establishing a binding standard? If not, then ijmāʿ and the probative force of naql were invented with the emergence of these sects — which is the height of absurdity, since naql and ijmāʿ would then be innovations. If, on the other hand, ijmāʿ and naql were binding before the emergence of these factions, then the emergence and dissent of these factions does not invalidate the prior ijmāʿ — just as the Christian defection into the doctrine of the Trinity and the abrogation of the Torah does not invalidate the ijmāʿ of all of humanity on monotheism and the eternal validity of the Torah; and just as the Samaritan defection from the post-Joshua prophets does not invalidate the ijmāʿ on the prophecy of the rest of the prophets and the orientation of prayer toward Jerusalem. So our companions' enumeration of the sects, and their counting them in to establish the validity of ijmāʿ, is senseless. The proper conclusion is: sound ijmāʿ is what the original total community held; and the defection of one, ten, or a hundred dissenters from it does not invalidate it.[{3}]

Another group of our companions held: naql and sound ijmāʿ are what is not ascribed to specific persons, and on which there is no scriptural text and no qiyās-derivation; rather, it is found in the hands of the community by oral instruction alone, from no other source. If a textual or analogical proof is available for it, then it is not ijmāʿ and not naql. But this definition is wrong. For say to its proponent: are not all the explicitly-textual commandments in Scripture (Sabbath, eating unleavened bread, circumcision, and the rest) also transmitted by the community and held by it in consensus? He must answer yes. Then it can be said: those commandments are known by two routes simultaneously — naṣṣ and naql/ijmāʿ. And what has two proofs is more secure than what has only one. So the position that "sound naql is only what has no textual or analogical proof" is incoherent: it would make naql the weakest form of knowledge by definition. Naql should be defined as what is attested by the community, regardless of whether it is also attested by text. (And some of our companions hold that the foundation of all ijmāʿ is in fact qiyās.)

Your point, then — that the correct naql and ijmāʿ are what are not ascribed to specific people but are found in the hands of the whole community as a whole — is the right view. The exemplary case: the consensus that today is the Sabbath, distinct from the other days of the week. This is not ascribed to any individual; it is received by transmission and inheritance; it is in the hands of the entire community from East to West, with no one having dissented from it across the ages. Moreover: this Sabbath-day consensus has not been inherited only by Israel; it is in the hands of all the nations — varied in their languages, lands, colors, lineages, and religions — who count the days starting from Sunday until they end at the seventh day (which is the Sabbath itself), which they name with their own languages by a term meaning "rest" / "Sabbath", then begin again from Sunday.[{4}] This is not the same as what some claim about Rosh Ḥodesh and the festival: that they are known by naql and ijmāʿ. The knowledge of the new moon and festivals reduces to calendrical intercalation (kibbus), which only a small number of people actually settle on. The intercalation in fact came originally from Shām to the Iraqis, until it became more widely known — together with the corruptions we have noted, and the contradictions in the statements of the school itself that show intercalation is not transmitted and not ancient; rather, it is an innovation introduced by a known individual — Ishaq Nephah.[{5}]

A parallel to the Sabbath as a case of sound consensus and transmission: the soundness of the text of the Torah and the rest of the prophetic books, which are in the hands of the whole community from East to West without dispute, without addition or subtraction, in a single recension. We do not find, in any of the manuscripts of the Torah, an added pericope or a deleted pericope. If a deletion occurs (in some particular copy), all parties agree that it is a scribal error; the entirety of the community has transmitted that judgment generation by generation, from the time of prophecy down to the present. So too the form of the Hebrew letters (the alphabet) and their order.

If someone counters with what we have reported of the Rabbanites — that this Torah is not the Torah that Moses brought, but a composition of Ezra's — we reply: their claim on that subject is on the same standing as their claim about other corrupt and false uṣūl and furūʿ; and their claim does not invalidate the sound naql — just as the defection of the Christians from the naql (which we already addressed) does not invalidate it. We will report their case and demonstrate its falsity in due course (§§19–20 below).

A further objection some might raise: what is reported in the codices about tikkun soferim (scribal emendations) — that eighteen passages in Scripture were altered by the scribes. If even one passage can be granted to have been altered, then many can have been; how then, given 18 reported cases? We will treat this objection in detail in Babs 21–22; for now: some of our companions have made this very fact into evidence for the soundness of the naql — for the alleged eighteen alterations were themselves noted and transmitted (the very claim that "X was altered to Y" presupposes the original was known); had other alterations occurred, they would have been likewise noted. So for them, this is one of the clearest proofs that no other alteration occurred. We ourselves do not go that route: we hold that the claim of an 18-alteration tikkun soferim is false. The matter never spread anciently among the codices; it appeared first in a few books and pamphlets, then expanded. Ancient codices show no trace of it; what trace there is, was taken from Rabbanite books — and Rabbanite books, as we have said, are not a source of naql or ijmāʿ. We will further demolish this position in Bab 22.

If someone further objects from ketib/qere — supposing this case to be analogous to tikkun soferim, since they appear in codices similarly, and some have rejected them (Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī and others) — let it be known that this supposition is mistaken. The difference between the two cases is plain: tikkun soferim spread recently; qere/ketib is not of that kind. There is consensus on it, and the naql of it is on par with the naql of the writing of the letters and the orthography of the agreed-on words (plene and defective), and with the naql of the trope and pause of reading. We will explain this in detail also.

What we have said about ijmāʿ on the Sabbath, the Torah, and the form and arrangement of the letters — the same applies to the naql of the translation of Scripture from Hebrew into other languages.[{6}] Most of the standard Arabic translations of common terms are by naql and ijmāʿ of the entire community: no one disputes that vayyikra means "and he called," vayyikkaḥ means "and he took," vayyaʿas means "and he made," vayyitten means "and he gave," YHWH is "the Lord," and Elohim is "the God." For every term of frequent occurrence, if you asked any of them what its rendering should be, they would give a non-disputed answer, not ascribed to any individual.

The unfamiliar terms of rare occurrence, however, are known only to some; those who translate them work by etymology, by semantic resonance, or by ascribing their rendering to specific authorities — e.g., the Ashkenazi, the Ramlī, Abraham b. Nūḥ, and others. These include the difficult terms of Nah 2:11 ("emptiness and waste"), Joel 1:17 ("the seeds have rotted"), many bird- and gemstone-names. On these, there is no naql and no ijmāʿ, and they admit disagreement. We have explained this in our treatise on translation (in a separate book). The translation of the text-as-a-whole cannot, however, be globally falsified: even if a hundred people gathered and tried to alter the rendering of a hundred verses word-by-word, they would not succeed — the Hebrew language and the syntactic-integration of statement would forbid it; what they fixed in one place would unravel in another; the rendering would not cohere. This is yet another piece of naql-stability.

This concludes our position on the uṣūl taken from sound naql and ijmāʿ — those that admit of no dispute and have no alternative route by which to acquire them. As for the furūʿ — the affirmative and negative laws, the licit and the forbidden, the general and the specific, and so on — what among these is naql and ijmāʿ is found in the news and reports of the [biblical] writings themselves. For example, the prohibition of carrying on the Sabbath out of the house or into it — as Jeremiah said (Jer 17:21): "Carry no burden out of your houses on the Sabbath day," and (v. 27): "Nor carry forth a burden out of your houses … nor bring it through the gates of Jerusalem." We are licit in moving objects of two or three raṭl within our houses; we are not licit in carrying out or in even a single dirham-weight. This is not in the naṣṣ, nor extracted by qiyās, nor known only by the prophetic khabar; but we know it of necessity, since the community has transmitted it from the days of Moses (peace upon him), preserved by the kingship and the prophecy.

So too for the prayer and its kayfiyya and times: David said (Ps 55:18), "Evening and morning and at noon will I pray, and cry aloud," and the parallel in Dan 6:11, 14: "three times a day…"; and orientation in prayer toward the Sanctuary — as Solomon said (1 Kgs 8:48), "and they shall pray to thee toward their land…," and as Daniel did (Dan 6:11), "and his windows were open in his upper chamber toward Jerusalem"; and the liturgical Psalter-tradition — as 2 Chr 29:30 reports, "[the Levites] sang praises unto the Lord with the words of David and of Asaph the seer"; and what is found in Ruth concerning redemption, the conditions of marriage, the removing of the shoe (Ruth 4:7).

Likewise the materials for the sukkah and the myrtle — not mentioned in the Torah but explained in the narrative of Ezra (Neh 8:14–16). Likewise the olive-press. Likewise the intercalation of the second Adar in the narrative of Hezekiah — "because the community had not gathered to Jerusalem" (2 Chr 30:3). Likewise the prohibition of "eating with the blood" (Lev 19:26), expounded in the narrative of Saul (1 Sam 14:33: "Behold the people sin against the Lord by eating with the blood"). Likewise the prohibition of eating things polluted with the dung of unclean animals, derived from the narrative of Ezekiel — Ezek 4:14, "ah, my soul has never been polluted," and God's response (v. 15), "Behold, I have given thee bullocks' dung…". Likewise that the moon is the cause of the festivals, as David said (Ps 104:19), "He made the moon for fixed times." Likewise the prohibition of speech on the Sabbath about non-Sabbath business, from Isa 58:13, "nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words." Likewise the prohibition for one married to a Gentile woman who repents and has children by her — that he must send out the wife and the children, from Ezra 10:3, "let us put away all the wives, and such as are born of them." Likewise the washing for menstrual impurity at sunset, from 2 Sam 11:4, "and she was cleansed from her impurity." Likewise the burning of the implements of idolatry, from 2 Kgs 23:4. Likewise the prohibition of eating the sacrifices of religious transgressors, from Ps 106:28: "and they ate the sacrifices of unbelievers." Likewise the case of Hag 2:12: "if a man carry holy flesh in the skirt of his garment"; and the bride-price and its being settled by mutual consent, from 2 Sam 3:14, "whom I betrothed to me for a hundred foreskins of the Philistines"; and that one who kills in war is not subject to retributive penalty, from 1 Kgs 2:5, "and he shed the blood of war in peace"; and the prohibition of praying while drunk, from 1 Sam 1:13, "Eli supposed her to be drunk"; and the narrative of Ezek 24:16, "Behold I take from thee the desire of thine eyes" — establishing custom (sunan) rather than command; and 2 Sam 11:11, "the ark and Israel and Judah"; and the posting of watchmen to prevent carrying in or out on the Sabbath, from Neh 13:19, "[so I set] some of my servants on the gates."

All of this — material in Scripture — is sound naql, of the kind we said is preserved by the community in concert with kingship and prophecy. As to what is not in this category — what we find not in Scripture, and not subject to refutation or impeachment, and that is transmitted in the hands of the community — we do not affirm it with full categorical certainty. The community was dispersed and broken, and those whom we have mentioned (the Rabbanites) ruled over them, altering and corrupting the texts we mentioned. If they could so alter the texts, they could all the more alter what is not in the texts. Nevertheless: in such cases, where what is found in the community's hands by ijmāʿ (and not in the text) tends in the direction of stringency and intensification (tashdīd wa-tathqīl), it is incumbent on us to adopt it and act on it; for we cannot be sure that it is not a sound naql, and if we fail to adopt it we may be culpable — provided the practice itself contains no internal corruption and is not ascribed to specific individuals or composed for self-interested gain. Examples: rules of slaughter and other farāʾiḍ that are intensifications, even if of Rabbanite composition (cf. Mishnah Ḥullin 1, "Rabbi Judah said in the name of Samuel: any slaughterer who does not know the rules of slaughter…") — these are not binding, since they are composed for self-interest. But the rules they advance about purity from evil, about not eating before the non-obligatory prayer, about the prohibition of piercing the ears of boys, about not riding a donkey in one's own house on the Sabbath, about not riding in a boat on a river within one's own property on the Sabbath, about the prohibition of eggs of unclean animals and eggs of forbidden birds — these are obligatory on us and to be observed. As to leniencies and "concessions" introduced by them — these are not to be followed. This is our position and our doctrine on naql and ijmāʿ, as it has become clear to us. We seek from God success and the manifestation of the truth. We now return (Bab 19) to what the Rabbanites have said: that the Torah, in the era of sovereignty, was not in fact in the hands of the whole community. ---
